newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka editor sentenced for defaming president.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka editor sentenced for defaming president.

text.p: A Sri Lankan newspaper editor was handed a suspended jail sentence of one year on Tuesday for criminal defamation of President Chandrika Kumaratunga.
Sinha Ratnatunga, editor of the Sunday Times, was found guilty of defaming Kumaratunga in an article published in the newspaper in 1995.
He said he would appeal against the verdict.

Colombo High Court Judge Upali de Z. Gunewardena also handed down a suspended sentence of six months to Ratnatunga for violating the Press Council Law, which deals with publication of incorrect information.
The case was brought against Ratnatunga after Kumaratunga complained to police that the article, which said she had attended a late night birthday party of a parliament deputy, was defamatory.
Kumaratunga says she never went to the party.
The verdict in the trial, which lasted 75 days, was read out in the court packed with journalists, lawyers and politicians.

The judge also fined Ratnatunga 7,500 rupees ($130) on the first count and 2,500 rupees ($43) on the second and said he would be liable to a total of seven months of imprisonment if he defaulted on the fines.
Ratnatunga told Reuters his lawyers planned to appeal against the verdict.
"Of course we are going to appeal. We are aggrieved by the order and we are appealing it," he said.
Deputy Solicitor General Rienzie Arasakularatne, who led the prosecution, said the Sunday Times article had lowered the president's reputation "in the eyes of the world".
"The assassination of a person's character is worse than the assassination of the person itself," he said.
Sri Lanka's ruling People's Alliance government has taken a tough stand against incorrect reporting of news.

In January, the government detained the director of a private television station for broadcasting what it said was a false news item about an attack by separatist Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam guerrillas on an eastern army camp.
The director was charged under the Prevention of Terrorism Act, but the charges were later dropped.
